text: How does a jet engine push an airliner through the sky? Let's take one apart.
This is a turbofan, the engine on almost every airliner. Its job: grab a huge amount of air, and throw it out the back, fast.
Up front, the giant fan. Most of the air it pulls in never enters the core. It flows around it. That's bypass air, and it makes most of the thrust.
The rest enters the core. Rows of compressor blades squeeze it, stage after stage, to over thirty times outside pressure.
In the combustor, fuel sprays into that squeezed air and burns nonstop, like a blowtorch that never goes out.
The hot gas blasts through the turbine and spins it. Shafts carry that power forward to drive the compressor and fan.
Then it rushes out the nozzle. Air goes back, so the engine goes forward. Newton's third law.
Suck, squeeze, bang, blow. All at once, all the time.
The Boeing 737's CFM fifty-six: a five-foot fan, about five times more air around the core than through it, and up to twenty-seven thousand pounds of thrust.
Congrats! You've discovered the jet engine.
